scope: 22 chapter study guides and 104 lesson sources, including objectives, math, main code, exercises/solutions, practice and primary figure guidance. Full narrative close reading was selective.
limits: No claim of independent human teaching acceptance.
Not every narrative sentence was independently proved.
No fresh execution of all lesson or project training programs.
No physical TPU, paid service or new model-quality campaign.
Existing dirty workspace content was preserved; findings refer to the isolated PR #71 source export, not all local uncommitted changes.
Project handoffs were inspected as dependencies of the lessons; this is not a fresh exhaustive execution audit of every project.

studyGuide.question: Can someone else reproduce your first result?
studyGuide.why: Start with one saved program and a known answer. The terminal, interpreter and working folder are part of the experiment: a notebook that imports a package is not yet proof that the downloaded script uses the same environment.

readiness.prompt: You saved a script in your course folder, but the terminal reports that the file does not exist. Which observation should you check first?
readiness.answer: Check the terminal’s current folder and the exact filename, including its extension. Then run the environment’s Python explicitly. Reinstalling JAX will not repair a wrong path.

milestones.title: Make one reproducible result
milestones.task: Run the row-sum example as a saved file. Record the Python executable, package versions, backend, input shape and computed sums. Explain why a package version alone cannot identify which interpreter ran the file.

milestones.title: Separate local practice from parallel TPU execution
milestones.task: Start a fresh process for virtual CPU devices and compare its device receipt with the ordinary process. Then learn how to get a TPU running (hosted TPU or single-host Cloud TPU VM), launch your experiment over SSH with explicit backend checks, and run subsequent course phases on TPU in parallel.

transfer.prompt: You have identical predictions on two computers, but one receipt says CPU and the other TPU. Which statements can you keep?
transfer.approach: Keep the tested numerical agreement and both environment records. Reject any claim of equal device performance: different compilation, synchronization and timing boundaries could explain differences. Reproduce one changed input before expanding the numerical claim.

pitfall.symptom: Import works in a notebook but fails in the terminal.

studyGuide.question: Can you spot a wrong axis even when the program runs?
studyGuide.why: Array bugs often return plausible numbers. Use unequal dimensions and hand-computed rows so that a successful operation cannot hide a mistaken meaning. Carry that habit into preprocessing and model inputs.

readiness.prompt: A matrix has three observations and two features. You need one mean per feature. Which axis should be reduced, and how many values remain?
readiness.answer: Reduce the observation axis, axis 0. Two feature means remain. Reducing axis 1 instead returns three observation means, which answers a different question.

milestones.title: Make preprocessing safe to reuse

transfer.prompt: Use rows \((1,3)\), \((5,7)\), \((100,200)\), with the last row masked. Predict feature means and population variances. Then select only the first row.
transfer.approach: With two valid rows the means are \((3,5)\), variances \((4,4)\), and count 2. Selecting only the first row gives means \((1,3)\), variances \((0,0)\), count 1. Dividing by all three rows is a denominator bug. A zero valid count needs rejection or an explicitly declared policy before division.

studyGuide.question: What changes when you differentiate, batch or compile a function?
studyGuide.why: Build one trustworthy scalar calculation before composing transformations. Differentiation changes the quantity, batching adds an axis, and compilation changes execution. Keeping these roles distinct makes later training failures easier to locate.

readiness.prompt: For a squared residual, is the gradient of the average loss the same shape as the stack of per-example gradients?
readiness.answer: No. A stack retains the examples axis; the gradient of the average reduces that axis. Their mean agrees for the same equally weighted differentiable objective.

milestones.title: Compose without changing the question

transfer.prompt: Two batches have sizes 2 and 6 and scalar mean gradients 3 and 1. What is the combined mean gradient? What mistake gives 2?
transfer.approach: The eight-example mean is \((2\cdot3+6\cdot1)/8=1.5\). Averaging the two batch means gives 2 and overweights the smaller batch. Compare with the gradient on concatenated examples, not another copy of the aggregation code.

studyGuide.question: Have you saved everything needed to determine the next step?
studyGuide.why: A program’s state includes random keys, counters and structured values as well as model parameters. Explicit ownership lets you reproduce a transition, run a batch safely, and later recover an interrupted experiment.

readiness.prompt: Two simulated examples receive the same random key and run the same sampling function. Should you expect independently allocated draws?
readiness.answer: No. The same key and operation replay the same draw in the tested environment. Split or derive distinct keys at the ownership boundary; unequal observed samples alone do not prove independence.

milestones.title: Audit repeated and conditional transitions

transfer.prompt: A random walk resumes with the correct position but a reset key. Its final mean is close to the uninterrupted result. Is that enough?
transfer.approach: No. A distribution-level agreement can coexist with different next draws. Compare the next random value, carry, step and later trajectory. Save the key at the same boundary as the position; do not claim cross-version bitwise reproducibility from a same-environment pass.

studyGuide.question: Can you explain an optimizer’s behavior from the objective and data?
studyGuide.why: Use a model small enough to solve independently. Connect residuals, gradients, curvature and update state before comparing optimizer names. A lower training loss is useful evidence, but it does not by itself establish better held-out predictions.

readiness.prompt: A model predicts one value for each observation. Targets accidentally have an extra trailing singleton axis. Why might mean squared error still run?
readiness.answer: Broadcasting can construct a pairwise residual matrix instead of one residual per observation. Assert identical prediction and target shapes, then compute one residual by hand before reducing.

transfer.prompt: For the scalar loss \(L(w)=w^2\), predict the next error multipliers for learning rates 0.4, 1.0 and 1.1. Which curve can oscillate without converging?
transfer.approach: The update is \(w_{t+1}=(1-2\eta)w_t\). The factors are \(0.2\), \(-1\) and \(-1.2\). The middle case alternates at constant magnitude; the last grows. A plotting window can hide divergence when the starting value is tiny. Check the recurrence and plot absolute error on a logarithmic scale where nonzero.

studyGuide.why: Move from explicit matrix operations to stateful modules while preserving independent checks. Learn to distinguish capacity, optimization, data quality and evaluation errors before adding layers.

readiness.prompt: A classifier predicts the majority class on every example and reports high accuracy. What information is missing?
readiness.answer: Class counts and per-class errors are missing. A majority baseline can score highly on imbalanced data while missing every rare example. Inspect the confusion matrix and the denominator for each class.

transfer.prompt: In a 100-example set, 95 labels are class zero and 5 are class one. A classifier always predicts zero. Interpret accuracy and rare-class recall.
transfer.approach: Accuracy is 95%, but class-one recall is \(0/5=0\). Record the confusion counts and compare against that constant baseline. Decide thresholds using validation data. Five rare examples leave substantial uncertainty, so the headline accuracy alone cannot establish useful rare-class behavior.

studyGuide.question: Can an interrupted run make exactly the same next update?
studyGuide.why: Recovery is a contract between data order, model state and publication. Tracking explains which run produced an artifact; a checkpoint supplies the values needed to continue it. Neither replaces the other.

readiness.prompt: The weights restore exactly, but the next loss differs. Which state should you inspect before blaming numerical nondeterminism?
readiness.answer: Compare optimizer moments and count, random keys, data permutation/cursor, preprocessing and configuration. The same weights with a different next batch are a different transition.

milestones.task: Inspect record IDs through shuffling and batching. State the final-batch policy and save iterator state only at the intended consumption boundary.

milestones.title: Prove a committed continuation
milestones.task: Save complete state, restore in a fresh process and compare future IDs and updates across an epoch boundary. Reject an incomplete or incompatible checkpoint before publishing it.

transfer.prompt: Two restored parameter arrays both have norm 5: \((3,4)\) and \((0,5)\). Did the checkpoint replay pass?
transfer.approach: No. Equal norms discard direction. Elementwise differences are \((3,-1)\), and the arrays can produce different predictions. Compare every required state leaf, the next batch IDs and subsequent updates under a declared tolerance, not only a norm or final scalar loss.

pitfall.symptom: The advertised checkpoint step is newer than the restored state.
pitfall.check: Inspect completion and publication order. An asynchronous save request is not proof that the artifact is durable or restorable.

studyGuide.question: Can you prove that a predicted token cannot see its future?
studyGuide.why: Attention is a weighted mixing operation whose axes and masks are testable. Build a causal model from these contracts before interpreting a generated sentence as evidence of learning.

readiness.prompt: A query has equal scores for three allowed keys. What are the attention weights, and what happens if one key is masked?
readiness.answer: The weights are equal thirds. Masking one key leaves equal halves on the two allowed keys and zero on the masked key. Normalize over keys, not queries.

milestones.title: Train, resume and decode one small model

transfer.prompt: Pack document A at positions 0 and 1 and document B at positions 2 and 3. Which keys may B’s first query use? What if A changes?
transfer.approach: With causal and same-segment masking, query 2 may use key 2 only, assuming it is a valid input. A pure causal mask incorrectly permits keys 0 and 1. Change A while keeping B fixed and require B outputs to remain unchanged. Align shifted targets so an end-of-document position does not learn the next document’s first token.

pitfall.symptom: Padding produces NaNs in attention.
pitfall.check: Count permitted keys in every query row. A fully masked softmax needs an explicit invalid-query policy; its output and loss must not become valid training evidence.

studyGuide.question: What measured evidence identifies the bottleneck?
studyGuide.why: Optimize a verified computation and a named timing boundary. Trace events, compiler estimates and wall-clock samples answer different questions; connect them before proposing a change.

readiness.prompt: A JAX call returns an array handle almost immediately. Does a timer ending there necessarily measure completed computation?
readiness.answer: No. Synchronize the result inside the measured boundary. Report first-call setup separately from warmed execution and keep inputs, dtype and output checks fixed.

transfer.prompt: A step takes 100 ms, of which one kernel takes 10 ms. That kernel becomes twice as fast while everything else stays fixed. Predict the new step time.
transfer.approach: The estimate is \(90+5=95\) ms, a speedup of about 1.053. A 2x kernel improvement is compatible with a small end-to-end gain. If the observed time differs, inspect the timing boundary, changed transfers, compilation and overlap rather than forcing the trace to fit the estimate.

pitfall.symptom: A claimed speedup disappears in repeated runs.
pitfall.check: Check equivalent work, compilation reuse, synchronization, sample spread and competing system activity; retain the raw samples.

studyGuide.question: Is the distributed update still optimizing the same objective?
studyGuide.why: Start with the global mathematical operation, then specify ownership and communication. Logical CPU devices help expose placement and reduction mistakes before you spend accelerator time.

readiness.prompt: Two devices see one and three valid examples. Should their mean gradients receive equal weight?
readiness.answer: No. Weight by valid example counts. Sum local gradient numerators and valid counts, then divide once. Padding and empty partitions must not silently change the denominator.

milestones.title: Verify placement and the global update
milestones.task: Inspect actual shard indices and compare each relevant output with an independent unpartitioned calculation, including padded and unequal partitions.

milestones.title: Connect communication and recovery

transfer.prompt: Three shards have valid counts 2, 6 and 0 and local gradient sums 6, 6 and 0. Predict the global mean and the empty-shard contribution.
transfer.approach: Reduce sums and counts separately: the global mean is \((6+6+0)/(2+6+0)=1.5\). The empty shard contributes a zero numerator and zero count; it must not compute \(0/0\). Reject a globally empty batch. Compare with an independent unsharded calculation.

pitfall.symptom: The gradient grows with device count.
pitfall.check: Check whether local means were summed without count normalization. Verify one complete update before interpreting a training curve.

studyGuide.question: Are you fitting the physical model or the solver’s error?
studyGuide.why: Use an analytic system to separate simulation correctness, numerical discretization and parameter inference. An accurate autodiff derivative can still belong to an inaccurate discretized model.

readiness.prompt: A solver’s output is differentiable. Does that establish that its gradient matches the continuous differential equation?
readiness.answer: No. Autodiff follows the implemented discrete steps. Compare a discrete reference and refine the step size toward an analytic or higher-accuracy continuous reference.

milestones.title: Validate dynamics and axes

milestones.title: Fit an identifiable inverse problem

transfer.prompt: Forward Euler solves \(y\prime=-y\) from 1 to time 1. Compare step sizes 0.5 and 0.25 with the exact exponential.
transfer.approach: Euler gives 0.25 for two half-steps and 0.31640625 for four quarter-steps. The exact value is about 0.36787944. The finer grid reduces this forward error; a correct derivative of either discrete program still need not equal the continuous derivative. Repeat at a fixed horizon and inspect convergence, rather than tuning the fitted parameter to hide solver error.

pitfall.symptom: The fitted rate changes as the time step is refined.
pitfall.check: Compare solver error and parameter estimates across resolutions before attributing the shift to physical variation.

studyGuide.completion: Use scientific-inverse. Keep discrete and continuous references, a refinement study, derivative checks, recovered parameters and a held-out/noise sensitivity report.

studyGuide.question: Which uncertainty does your model actually represent?
studyGuide.why: Use an exactly solvable Bayesian regression to check inference. Separate uncertainty about weights, uncertainty about a future observation, and mismatch between the assumed likelihood and the data.

readiness.prompt: Should an interval for a new noisy observation equal an interval for the latent mean prediction?
readiness.answer: No. The observation includes additional likelihood noise. Under the independent Gaussian model, add its variance to the latent predictive variance before taking a square root.

milestones.title: Build an exact reference
milestones.task: Keep distribution units and normalization, derive a posterior in a small solvable case and compare latent versus observation uncertainty.

milestones.title: Challenge approximate inference
milestones.task: Compare sampler moments with the exact target, inspect multiple-chain diagnostics and measure the covariance lost by a diagonal approximation. Use predictive residuals to challenge the likelihood itself.

transfer.prompt: A correlated Gaussian target has unit marginal variances and correlation 0.8. A diagonal Gaussian variational fit gets the mean right but reports variance 0.36. Must optimization have failed?
transfer.approach: Not necessarily. In the reverse-KL Gaussian case the optimal diagonal variances equal inverse precision diagonals, which here are \(1-0.8^2=0.36\). The family cannot represent correlation. Compare mean, covariance and predictive intervals with the exact target; a small optimizer gradient does not certify uncertainty calibration.

pitfall.symptom: Intervals are narrow and diagnostics look reassuring despite poor predictions.
pitfall.check: Check whether you plotted latent or observation uncertainty, and whether the likelihood or mean function misses structure.

studyGuide.completion: Use bayesian-regression. Retain analytic posterior checks, sampler/approximation diagnostics and a predictive model-mismatch case, with uncertainty assumptions stated.

studyGuide.why: Environment semantics and data collection define the learning problem. Verify transitions, masks and behavior-policy probabilities before trusting a noisy return curve.

readiness.prompt: An episode stops because its time budget expires. Must its bootstrap value be zero?
readiness.answer: Not necessarily. Distinguish truncation from genuine terminal states and state whether the task is finite-horizon or continuing. A timeout alone does not imply that future value is zero.

transfer.approach: The true terminal target is 1. A cutoff that only ends data collection can retain bootstrap value, giving \(1+0.9\cdot10=10\). Use the final pre-reset observation, not a new episode’s reset observation. Declare the task semantics: a genuinely finite-horizon terminal objective can require a different contract. Verify boundary handling and sentinel values with the API supported by the kernel. studyGuide.question: Which mathematical operation does the transformed program represent?
studyGuide.why: Use internal representations to explain and verify transformations, not to memorize printed variable names. Separate primal values, tangent directions, cotangents and compiled artifacts.

readiness.prompt: A function maps an input vector to an output vector. Does a JVP multiply by the Jacobian or its transpose?
readiness.answer: A JVP maps an input tangent through the Jacobian. A VJP maps an output cotangent through its transpose. Check the spaces and the adjoint inner-product identity.

transfer.prompt: A proposed JVP returns \(2xv^2\) for \(f(x)=x^2\). It agrees at direction 1. Test direction 2 and explain the failure.
transfer.approach: The correct derivative map is \(2xv\). At direction 2 the proposal gives \(8x\) instead of \(4x\), except at the uninformative base point zero. Test nonzero base points and linear combinations of directions, then compare against an independent primal derivative.

pitfall.symptom: A derivative test passes at one input but fails after a shift.
pitfall.check: Inspect captured constants, detached values and custom rules. Compare both primal and derivative behavior at changed base points.

studyGuide.why: A deployment includes preprocessing, parameter layout, numeric policy and runtime behavior. Verify the same raw examples across each boundary before comparing memory or speed.

readiness.prompt: Weights match after conversion, but predictions differ. What besides weights must be compared?
readiness.answer: Compare input normalization, feature/channel order, operation semantics, non-trainable state, output labels, dtype and shape. Start with a hand-computed asymmetric example to expose layout mistakes.

milestones.task: Package and qualify the selected service, relate queue assumptions to measured service work, then examine the additional conversion and device budgets for an edge target. Leave actual device fields unmeasured until tested. Keep separate artifact, process, image and device receipts. Explain an interpolated percentile and a burst deadline failure before choosing a capacity intervention.

transfer.prompt: Frozen calibration maps [-1, 1] to signed integers. New inputs include 3. Explain why a small weight-file size says little about prediction quality or speed.
transfer.approach: The out-of-range activation must follow the declared clipping or fallback policy. Track saturation by channel and compare the same preprocessed input with the float reference. Storage savings do not show native integer execution. Measure actual runtime placement and latency after numerical and quality gates pass.

pitfall.symptom: A smaller model file produces no lower request latency.
pitfall.check: Inspect load-time expansion, fallback operators, transfers and preprocessing on the named runtime. File size is not a kernel or latency measurement.

studyGuide.question: Can you detect, explain and safely recover a failed model release?
studyGuide.why: Operational evidence connects work done to user-visible behavior. Separate worker health, model quality and release ownership so an alert leads to a specific investigation rather than automatic retraining.

readiness.prompt: A worker process is alive but has emitted no progress for a long time. Is it healthy?
readiness.answer: Liveness only establishes that the process exists or responds. Check readiness, last completed work, expected duration and checkpoint freshness before choosing a bounded timeout or recovery action.

transfer.approach: Keep the previous accepted artifact active and retain the failed candidate’s evidence. A global average cannot override a required slice gate. Record artifact/config identity and the reason for rejection. Test that a failed promotion leaves the active selection unchanged; rollback must select a verified prior artifact, not simply a filename.

issues.title: [P1][Content] Align value-fitting targets with the discount used by the GAE example
issues.problem:
The code fits its value table to `returns_to_go`, an undiscounted reverse cumulative sum, and then feeds this table to GAE with `gamma=0.9`. The lesson does not introduce this as an intentional mismatched value approximation or explain its effect on TD residuals.

A deterministic two-transition example exposes the difference. Rewards `[1,1]`, terminal V=0, and undiscounted values `[2,1,0]` give TD residuals `[-0.1,0]` at gamma=.9. The matched discounted values `[1.9,1,0]` give `[0,0]`. Lower regression error on undiscounted targets does not make this a matched discounted critic.

This does not mean GAE may never use an approximate critic, or that gamma must always equal one. The position-only value table's missing remaining-time state is already disclosed and should remain disclosed. The [GAE paper](https://arxiv.org/html/1506.02438v6) distinguishes discounted value definitions and discount/variance choices.
acceptance: State the objective, discount, horizon and value target before fitting the table.
Either fit discounted targets consistent with gamma, use gamma=1 for the stated undiscounted task, or explicitly teach the mismatch as a controlled approximation with its consequences.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Connect model sharding to a per-device memory-fit exercise
issues.problem:
The distributed chapter executes meaningful 1D data sharding, weighted gradients and collectives, but its opening 2D data/model notation never becomes a parameter-sharded learner step. The TPU capacity exercises still ask whether aggregate HBM means a model fits, despite newer prose and starter invariants correctly saying it does not prove per-device fit.

A 48 GiB replicated state does not fit on any 16 GiB device in a 4-device slice, although aggregate HBM is 64 GiB. Ideal full sharding gives 12 GiB/device before activations, temporaries, uneven partitions and headroom. The existing exercise explanation silently assumes sharding without proving placement.

`tpu-01` also equates device_count('tpu') with chip count without a topology qualifier. Its own newer chapter transfer discusses generations/chiplets where those terms must be distinguished. [JAX's TPU hardware reference](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/pallas/tpu/hardware.html) distinguishes chip and TensorCore-level hardware; use topology-specific API observations rather than a universal device-to-chip identity.
acceptance: Add a bounded 2x2 logical-CPU mesh exercise with explicit parameter, batch and optimizer-state placement, followed by one real forward/backward/update comparison to an unsharded oracle.
Record per-device shapes/bytes and collective ownership; include unequal or empty valid-count cases and explain the reduction axes.
Replace aggregate-fit conclusions with replicated-versus-sharded per-device ledgers and explicit peak/headroom assumptions.
Teach topology-specific process/device/chip terminology and verify it against the selected generation/API receipt.
Add training-versus-inference sizing decisions, keeping training state and inference KV cache separate.
Keep logical CPU execution distinct from physical TPU qualification and do not require a new paid hardware run to complete the teaching task.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Extend framework parity from Dense/MLP layers to attention and sequence semantics
issues.problem: There is already an optional real Keras backend lab and an actual PyTorch-to-NNX MLP/LayerNorm conversion with epsilon and gradient checks. These are useful foundations. The promised conversion skill still lacks the Transformer-specific failure modes learners face with saved language/embedding models: fused QKV layout, head axes, positions, masks, processor identity and tied embeddings.
acceptance: Add a small saved Transformer conversion using the existing chapter architecture, with an explicit source-to-target tensor/name/layout map.
Compare asymmetric-input intermediate activations in execution order and report the first divergent layer, absolute/relative error and tolerance rationale.
Include a nonuniform input-gradient/VJP check, mask/position parity and save/reload into a fresh process.
Inject one QKV/head-layout error and one semantic processor/mask error that cannot be caught by shape checks alone.
Pin versions and identify the bounded architecture. Preserve optional-framework installation and do not imply support for every checkpoint family.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Bridge masked and contrastive mechanics to held-out saved-encoder exercises
issues.problem:
The three lessons explain their limited fixtures honestly and include useful independent checks. MLM uses three repeated-token sequences; MIM uses a fixed visible-patch linear decoder; contrastive retrieval is evaluated on four training pairs. These teach objectives, but do not establish learned representation transfer or guide the learner through a saved mask-aware encoder.

The PR stack already contains a saved embedding pilot and image project material. Reuse those foundations and their declared evidence limits instead of duplicating another toy objective or claiming a production model has passed.
acceptance: Add an explicit small-model route with stage inputs, data recipe, split/source-group policy, tokenizer or patch transform, mask schedule, objective and artifact outputs.
For MLM require a learner-controlled corruption/objective change and held-out masked loss against a declared baseline, then a frozen-encoder downstream probe.
For MIM vary the mask and distinguish visible encoding from target reconstruction; explain what the frozen representation probe can and cannot show.
For contrastive learning include held-out groups, multiple positives and false-negative handling; compare retrieval metrics against an independent ranking reference.
Keep data/model/processor/checkpoint identity across stages and link each transfer task to the existing pilot files and prerequisites.
Do not require a new 300M run or relabel failed/unperformed project-quality gates. Full production lifecycles remain in #29.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Provide a guided sequence-model handoff for SFT, reward learning and DPO
issues.problem:
The current mechanics are useful and their limitations are disclosed: SFT trains a token transition table that cannot use earlier context, reward ranking uses three training comparisons, and DPO operates on a three-action table. A saved-decoder PPO appendix now exists and reports a failed quality result; it must not be erased or represented as a pass.

The missing teaching step is a required, bounded route that carries a saved sequence model from the existing causal/foundations pilot through learner edits and held-out checks. An optional appendix link alone does not tell learners how to transfer the objective and evidence contracts.
acceptance: Give a small saved-decoder transfer checklist with exact prerequisite, model/tokenizer identity, input/output artifact and one learner-controlled change at each stage.
Score unequal-length responses using summed token log probabilities, shifted response masks and padding rules; compare a hand calculation and an independent reference.
Add held-out prompts, preference disagreement slices, reward-scale sensitivity and retention evaluation, with baselines defined before updates.
Connect the existing PPO appendix with a changed-condition analysis task that preserves its failed quality result and explicitly separates objective optimization from response usefulness.
Keep full production training/release work in #29; this issue can be completed with a bounded teaching fixture and retained evidence, without launching a new model-quality campaign.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Make the LoRA adapter artifact enforce the base identity taught in prose
issues.problem:
The prose correctly requires base checkpoint hash, target modules, rank, alpha and dtype. The adapter-save exercise writes only A, B, alpha and rank, then reloads against the live base variable. There is no bound base identity or wrong-base rejection. A shape-compatible different base can silently produce a different model.

The current fitted-base, gradient asymmetry, nonunit scaling and merge checks should be retained. This issue closes the gap between the stated artifact contract and its implementation.
acceptance: Save a manifest binding adapter tensors to an identified base checkpoint, target modules, shapes, dtype, rank and scaling convention.
Reload the base and adapter independently in a fresh process and compare unmerged versus merged predictions on changed inputs.
Reject a shape-compatible wrong base and altered metadata before activation; explain why matching tensor shapes is insufficient.
Include a nonunit alpha/r case and preserve evidence that base parameters remain frozen during adaptation.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Connect MLOps and LLMOps gates to actual prediction and trace evidence
issues.problem:
The MLOps lesson has useful group-leakage and weighted-slice counterexamples, but receives supplied squared errors rather than computing predictions from a reloaded artifact. The LLMOps lesson records real MLflow spans and missing/critical-case bookkeeping, but nine answerable fixtures are duplicates and answers are canned; no prompt/model/retrieval stage produces them. Existing replay labeling is honest and should remain.

Learners need one connected offline workflow to show what is evaluated, where a response failed and why a release gate changes. Paid APIs are unnecessary for this task.
acceptance: Evaluate a reloaded local artifact and derive per-example and slice metrics from predictions/targets, preserving group-safe splits and weighting.
Provide heterogeneous stable case IDs with supported, unsupported, missing, duplicate and out-of-order responses; demonstrate a case that changes the release decision.
Trace actual local prompt/retrieval/model boundaries using a bounded local adapter, or clearly identify an immutable captured replay and its limits.
Have the learner localize one retrieval failure, one answer-generation failure and one infrastructure failure from trace/metric evidence.
Require a changed candidate comparison with the same case IDs, denominators, policy and artifact identity. Do not equate drift alone with model quality.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Demonstrate behavioral rollback and model retirement in the release lessons
issues.problem:
Release A and B in operations-04 differ in metadata rather than model behavior. The test proves pointer/content selection, but does not show a consumer restoring the previous model's predictions. Operations-08 includes retirement in its title while its implementation/exercises stop at activation, approval expiry and target checks.

Current content-bound approval and side-effect-free rejection are good foundations. The missing learner outcome is a complete, clearly scoped lifecycle with observed consumer behavior and retirement semantics.
acceptance: Use two identified, valid artifacts with intentionally different predictions and a consumer that loads the selected artifact.
Record predictions before activation, after activation and after rollback; demonstrate that a rejected activation leaves behavior and selection unchanged.
Define and exercise retirement/tombstone behavior for active and fallback versions, including cache/reload and rollback eligibility.
Add stale approval, retired target and expired approval negative cases plus an audit trail tied to exact bundle identity.
Keep the single-writer/local/no-auth scope explicit and avoid presenting pointer files as a production access-control system.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Stage long operations and recovery listings around the concept being learned
issues.problem:
Operations-01 through -05 each embed roughly 192-255 lines, including about 180 lines of shared supervisor/worker scaffolding, while often offering only three build steps. The new concept is difficult to locate in repeated code. Recovery-03/-04 similarly place pack/version helpers before the state/iterator replay story.

This is a teaching-structure issue, not a request to remove runnable programs or weaken process-isolation tests. Learners should be able to explain the mechanism without reverse-engineering the entire support harness first.
acceptance: Identify reviewed support code versus learner-authored transitions and show a short concept-focused excerpt first.
Add a worked execution/state trace and explain each new boundary before presenting the full program.
Reuse a versioned common support module in downloadable exercises, or clearly show deltas while keeping each download runnable.
Require a small change that tests the central concept and an interpretation task using actual logs/state transitions.
Verify script/notebook/book parity and fresh-download execution after reorganizing the teaching material.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Add concept-specific diagrams where current plots do not show the mechanism
issues.problem:
Many figures now have useful reading guidance. A few remaining visuals show an outcome without making the chapter's main mechanism visible:

- tpu-01 puts chip counts and GiB on one "count / capacity" axis. Separate units and show process/device/chip ownership.
- networks-02 uses anonymous leaf indices. Show module paths, GraphDef/State separation and shared versus copied state.
- transforms-05 sum/mean bars do not show specialization. Add a signature-to-trace ledger with value-only and shape/static changes.
- rl-05 critic-loss plot does not explain the reverse GAE scan. Add time steps, terminal/cutoff observations, bootstrap and trace masks with a hand-computed value chain.
- kernels-03 memory bars do not show pipeline scheduling. Add buffer-lifetime/load/compute/store overlap with prologue, steady state and drain.
- transforms-02 overlays loss and derivative with different units on one axis. Split panels while keeping matching x coordinates and the zero-gradient interpretation.

Use deterministic SVG/Mermaid/standard plots for exact tensors, timelines and values. Decorative generated images cannot establish these relationships.
acceptance: Generate each figure from the exact fixture or an explicitly labeled schematic and define axes, units, arrows, masks and legends.
Explain one specific observation and why it follows from the code/math, plus a prediction question for a changed input.
Include a numerical/structural check for plotted labels and a text equivalent conveying the same mechanism.
Check narrow reader, downloadable HTML, print and EPUB legibility. Keep existing useful plots where they answer a different question.

issues.title: [P2][Content] Expose lesson-level prerequisites and a clear CPU-first setup route
issues.problem:
The Setup route introduces Mesh, PartitionSpec, jit and addressable shards before those concepts are taught. It has hardware cues marking advanced setup as optional, but needs an explicit beginner continuation path and a small placement explanation.

The post-training PPO prose tells learners to complete RL-01 through RL-04, with RL-05 useful for the value/GAE bridge. Those cross-phase dependencies are not represented by the posttraining-04 lesson prerequisite, which names only posttraining-03. Do not force all RL prerequisites on SFT/LoRA, which do not need them.
acceptance: Represent the PPO lesson cross-phase dependencies in canonical metadata and show them in lesson/chapter entry guidance.
Provide a CPU-first beginner branch through setup, with virtual-device/TPU setup explicitly deferred until its conceptual prerequisites.
Add a brief readiness task for array shapes, pure transforms, rollout masks and policy objectives at the relevant handoffs.
Verify that pathway order and book navigation preserve these dependencies without creating cycles or blocking unrelated lessons.
